1121.title: Natural law (CCC 1954–1960)
1121.hook: a moral sense written in human reason, shared across cultures
1121.howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching appeals to natural law when speaking with people of every faith or none, arguing from reason as well as from scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, subsidiarity: the larger community helps, and doesn't take over. Your line was closest hands first.

Two small children at a playground, on holiday, from two different countries. They share no language at all. They've been taking turns on the slide, and it's working. Then one cuts in front. The other doesn't need a single word: hands on hips, a frown, a finger pointing back at the line. Everybody watching understands it at once: that's not fair. Nobody taught them the same rulebook, the same religion, or any religion. And still each recognized the same wrong. Paul noticed something like this, writing to the Christians in Rome.
screen: `NO SHARED LANGUAGE.` → `ONE CUTS THE LINE.` → `THAT'S NOT FAIR.`

segments.voice: The phrase is natural law. Not the laws of nature, like gravity: a moral law. The Catechism says it expresses the original moral sense that lets a person tell, by reason, good from evil, and truth from a lie. It quotes Saint Thomas Aquinas: the natural law is the light of understanding placed in us by God, by which we know what we must do and what we must avoid. God gave this light, Thomas says, at creation. Why natural? Not because animals follow it, but because reason, which declares it, belongs to human nature. Paul, writing about people who never received the law of Moses, says that when they do by nature what the law asks, they show, in the Douay-Rheims, "the work of the law written in their hearts." The natural law, the Catechism says, is present in the heart of each person, and it quotes the Roman writer Cicero: there is a true law, right reason, in agreement with nature, spread among all people. How it's applied varies, and takes reflection, across places, times and circumstances. But the law itself is unchanging through history; even when it's denied, it can't be destroyed or erased from the human heart. It always rises again. Last, an honest limit. Not everyone sees its precepts clearly and at once. That's why, the Catechism says, people need grace and revelation too, so moral truth can be known easily, firmly and without error. Tomorrow picks up that word, grace.
screen: `NOT GRAVITY: A MORAL SENSE.` · `A LIGHT OF UNDERSTANDING FROM GOD.` · `WRITTEN IN THEIR HEARTS.` · `NOT ALWAYS SEEN CLEARLY.`

segments.voice: Think of something people react to the same way across ages and backgrounds, someone cheated, a promise broken, a child treated cruelly, a stranger who stopped to help, and stay with it. Notice whether you had to look it up, and whether it shows up anywhere in the body, or nowhere at all. If you pray, give thanks for that light; if you don't, let it be there a moment longer.
Natural law. The moral sense written in human reason, by which people tell good from evil: in the Catechism's words, a light of understanding placed in us by God. Today's word.

1122.title: Grace and merit (CCC 2006–2011)
1122.hook: even our merits are God's gifts
1122.howItsDone: Catholics are taught that every good work begins with God's grace; some end the day with an examen, thanking God for the good done and asking pardon for the rest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, natural law: a moral sense the Catechism says is written in human reason. Your line was written in reason.

A seven-year-old comes home from the dollar store with a birthday present for her father: a mug that says world's okayest dad, wrapped in the comics page with far too much tape. He opens it and acts as if it's gold. Nobody mentions that the money for the mug came from him, and so did the ride to the store. In a sense, he paid for his own present. And still, the gift is completely hers, and he's completely delighted.
screen: `A MUG FROM THE DOLLAR STORE.` → `WHO PAID FOR IT?` → `STILL COMPLETELY HERS.`

segments.voice: Back in year one you met grace itself. Today, what grace does with our work. Merit, the Catechism says, is the reward a community owes someone for what they've done: fair pay for fair work. Then it turns the word around. Before God, nobody has a strict right to merit anything. The gap between Creator and creature is too wide; everything we have, we first received. So where does merit come from? From God's free plan to bring people into the work of his grace. Grace goes first: the free gift that makes a good act possible. Then the person freely says yes and acts, and God, who gave the strength, rewards the act. The order matters: the merit of good works belongs first to God's grace, and then to the person who acted. The Catechism quotes Augustine, paraphrased: our merits are God's gifts. And a prayer of the Mass: in crowning the merits of his saints, God crowns his own gifts. Paul says it in the Douay-Rheims: "By the grace of God, I am what I am." He worked harder than the others, he adds, yet not he, but God's grace with him. The Catechism calls the charity of Christ the source in us of all our merits. And it gives the last word to Thérèse of Lisieux, who wrote that at the evening of her life she would come before God with empty hands, not asking him to count her works, and wanting to be clothed in his own justice. Merit isn't a ledger. It's a gift that becomes ours, and then goes home.
screen: `MERIT: WHAT A COMMUNITY OWES.` · `BEFORE GOD, GRACE GOES FIRST.` · `HE CROWNS HIS OWN GIFTS.` · `THÉRÈSE: EMPTY HANDS.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last few days to one good thing you actually did, maybe small, a call returned, a hard truth said kindly. See it plainly, without shrinking or polishing it, and ask where it came from: the strength, the moment, the person who taught you how. If you pray, thank God for it as his gift working in you; if not, simply hold it with gratitude.
Grace and merit. Grace goes first, a free gift; merit is the good we freely do with it, counted first to his grace and then to us. Today's word.
Your line: his gift in us. Thanks can be yours and his at once. Until tomorrow.

1123.title: The precepts of the Church (CCC 2041–2043)
1123.hook: Sunday Mass, yearly confession, Easter communion, fasting, support
1123.howItsDone: Catholics are taught the five precepts in catechism classes; parishes post the holy days and the fasting days each year, and the precepts tie a Catholic's year to Sunday, Lent and Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace and merit: grace goes first, and even our merits are God's gifts. Your line was his gift in us.

Folding chairs, a box of donuts, a whiteboard marker running dry: a confirmation class in a church basement. A fifteen-year-old in the back raises his hand with a question others may be wondering too: okay, but what's the least I have to do to still count? The catechist laughs, and then, instead of dodging, she writes a short list on the board. Five lines. Today's word is that list, and the surprising way the Church itself describes it.
screen: `A CHURCH BASEMENT, TUESDAY NIGHT.` → `WHAT'S THE LEAST I HAVE TO DO?` → `FIVE LINES ON A WHITEBOARD.`

segments.voice: In your first weeks you met Sunday, the obligation nobody explains as a gift. Here is the whole list it belongs to. The Catechism calls them the precepts of the Church, five of them. First: attend Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation, and rest from work that gets in the way of keeping the day holy. Second: confess your sins at least once a year. Third: receive Communion at least during the Easter season. Fourth: keep the days of fasting and abstinence the Church sets. Fifth: help provide for the needs of the Church, each according to their ability. The Catechism doesn't present the precepts as the goal of the Christian life. It calls them positive laws meant to guarantee a very necessary minimum: the least a Catholic owes in prayer and moral effort, so that love of God and neighbor has room to grow. A floor, not a ceiling. Think of them as the bones of a year: every week a Sunday; every year a confession and an Easter Communion; fasting days, when what the body wants comes second for a while; and the collection basket, or time and skills given instead, so the parish lights stay on and the poor are fed. Each one ties a private life to the life of the whole Church. So the honest answer to what's the least I have to do is this list. And the honest follow-up is that the least is only where it starts. Nobody falls in love and asks how few dinners they can get away with.
screen: `THE FIVE PRECEPTS.` · `SUNDAY, CONFESSION, EASTER, FASTING, SUPPORT.` · `A VERY NECESSARY MINIMUM.` · `A FLOOR, NOT A CEILING.`

segments.voice: Go through the five slowly, one line at a time: Sunday, confession, Easter Communion, fasting days, supporting the community. For each, notice where you are with it right now, without scolding yourself; if you're not Catholic, ask what your own small minimum is, the few things you keep no matter what. If you pray, ask for help with the one that's hardest.

1124.title: First commandment (CCC 2084–2141)
1124.hook: faith, hope and love of God, and no superstition
1124.howItsDone: Catholics learn the commandments in catechism and use them in an examination of conscience before confession; the first is kept through prayer, the Mass, and trusting God over luck and fortune-telling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the precepts: five basic duties, a floor and not a ceiling. Your line was the minimum, not the maximum.

A phone lights up at 7 a.m. with a daily horoscope: avoid big decisions, the stars are not on your side. On a dashboard, a little charm swings from the mirror. In a drawer, the lucky socks from the playoff game. None of it looks like religion. Maybe a joke, maybe a half-belief. The first commandment has something to say about all of that, and about a great deal more.
screen: `A HOROSCOPE AT 7 A.M.` → `A CHARM ON THE MIRROR.` → `THE LUCKY SOCKS.`

segments.voice: Back in year one you met the Ten Commandments as a whole. Now the Catechism walks through them one at a time. In Exodus, God speaks first about what he has done, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." Only then the command: "Thou shalt not have strange gods before me." Rescue first, then the rule. The Catechism reads it as a call to the three virtues aimed straight at God. Faith: trusting God and what he has revealed. Hope: expecting from him the help to love him and reach the life he promises. Charity: loving God above everything, for his own sake. In the desert, Jesus answers the tempter with words the Catechism places here: "The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve." Adoration, prayer, sacrifice and promises kept to God all put him first. Then it names what pushes God out of first place. Idolatry: making a god of anything that isn't God, which can be power, pleasure, race, ancestors, the state, money. Divination: horoscopes, astrology, palm reading, mediums, all trying to grab hold of the future instead of trusting it to God. And superstition, described carefully: not only lucky charms, but treating even good religious practices as if they worked like magic, by their outward form alone. A medal, a novena, a candle are not the problem. Thinking they force God's hand is. In this reading, the first commandment is a question of order: whatever sits first in a life is what that life serves.
screen: `RESCUE FIRST, THEN THE RULE.` · `FAITH, HOPE AND LOVE OF GOD.` · `IDOLATRY AND DIVINATION.` · `SUPERSTITION: GOOD THINGS USED AS MAGIC.`

segments.voice: If there's one, let a small habit you lean on for luck come to mind: a ritual before a game, a number you avoid, a chain message forwarded just in case. Ask what it's really asking for, safety, control, a good outcome, and notice that wish underneath the habit. If you pray, hand the same wish to God directly; if not, simply set the habit down for today.
First commandment. Thou shalt not have strange gods before me: faith, hope and love aimed at God first, and no idol, fortune-telling or superstition in his place. Today's word.
Your line: god first. The commandments start with a rescue, not a rule. Until tomorrow.

1125.title: Second commandment (CCC 2142–2159)
1125.hook: the holy name, and your own name too
1125.howItsDone: Catholics are taught to speak God's name with reverence; at baptism a child receives a Christian name, which may be a saint's, and the priest baptizes in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first commandment: faith, hope and love aimed at God, and no luck charm in his place. Your line was god first.

The coffee shop is loud. The barista slides a cup across the counter and calls out a name that's almost yours, spelled the way no one has ever spelled it. Later that week, at a funeral, a grandson reads his grandmother's full name aloud, every part of it, slowly, and the room goes still. Same thing, a name: in one place scribbled and forgotten, in the other held like something precious. Today's commandment is about a name, God's, and it ends up being about yours.
screen: `A NAME MISSPELLED ON A CUP.` → `A FULL NAME READ AT A FUNERAL.` → `GOD'S NAME, AND YOURS.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain." The Catechism begins with a gift: God entrusts his name to those who believe in him, as he told Moses his name at the burning bush. To give someone your name is to let them call on you. So the commandment asks for the respect you'd give the name of someone you love. Then it names what goes against it. Blasphemy: words of hatred or contempt aimed at God, the Church or the saints. Using God's name to cover crimes, or to justify violence against a people. Careless swearing, where the holiest name becomes filler. And a false oath: calling on God as witness to a lie. Jesus goes further in the Sermon on the Mount: don't swear at all; let your yes mean yes. The Church still allows an oath for a serious and just reason, like testimony in court. A person is baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and receives their own name in the Church. God calls each one by name, the Catechism says, and everyone's name is sacred: the icon of the person, a sign of the dignity of the one who bears it. In Revelation, the one who overcomes is promised a white stone with a new name on it, known only to the one who receives it. So the second commandment guards two names at once: the name above every name, and the one on your coffee cup.

Then say your own name, quietly, as though someone kind were saying it to you.

1126.hook: Sunday rest, worship and time for family and the poor

Sunday, 9:14 p.m. An email lands with the subject line: quick question. It isn't quick, and it isn't really a question. The laptop opens, and the evening is gone. Somewhere else, a family has had pancakes, gone to Mass, visited an aunt in a nursing home, and is now arguing cheerfully over a board game. Both are Sundays. Only one looks different from the other six days. This is the commandment that sets a day apart.
screen: `SUNDAY, 9:14 P.M.` → `QUICK QUESTION.` → `A DAY THAT LOOKS DIFFERENT.`

segments.voice: You met Sunday in your first weeks and the Sabbath in year one. In the Douay-Rheims: "Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day." The Catechism roots it in creation: God worked six days and rested on the seventh. Rest isn't laziness; it's something God himself is pictured doing. In Jewish tradition, the Sabbath is the seventh day, and the Catechism honors it as a sign of the covenant and a day of freedom, when even servants and animals rest. Jesus keeps the Sabbath, and in Mark he says: "Therefore the Son of man is Lord of the sabbath also." Christians came to gather on the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection, the Lord's Day. The Catechism quotes Justin Martyr, an early Christian writer, on believers gathering on the day of the sun; in the same passage, Justin describes people from town and country meeting on Sunday to hear the apostles' writings and share the Eucharist. So the Catholic Sunday has two sides. Worship: Catholics are obliged to take part in Mass on Sundays and holy days, unless excused for a serious reason like illness or the care of infants. And rest: avoiding work or business that gets in the way of worship, joy, works of mercy and the relaxation of mind and body. Then the circle widens: time for family, often scattered during the week; for the sick and the elderly; for silence and study. And a line for employers and every Christian: don't make needless demands that keep others from keeping the Lord's Day. Rest, here, isn't only for you.
screen: `GOD RESTED ON THE SEVENTH DAY.` · `LORD OF THE SABBATH ALSO.` · `THE LORD'S DAY: MASS AND REST.` · `TIME FOR FAMILY AND THE POOR.`

1127.title: Fourth commandment (CCC 2197–2257)
1127.hook: honor parents, and parents and leaders serve those in their care
1127.howItsDone: Catholics are taught to honor and care for their parents throughout life; parents promise at a child's baptism to raise them in the faith, and the Church calls the family a domestic church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third commandment: Sunday, kept with worship, rest, and time for others. Your line was keep holy the day.

A plastic pill organizer, seven little doors, morning and night. On a weeknight, a woman in her forties fills it for her father. He watches from the doorway, a little embarrassed, a little grateful. Forty years ago, he was the one cutting her grapes in half so she wouldn't choke. Neither of them says anything about it. The roles have quietly turned over. The fourth commandment lives right there, in the turning.

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Honour thy father and thy mother." The Catechism says this commandment opens the second part of the law, the part about neighbors, and it starts at home, in the family it calls a domestic church. For children, honor means respect, gratitude and, while they live at home, obedience. And it doesn't expire: grown children owe their parents help in old age, sickness, loneliness and distress, as far as they can. The book of Sirach, which the Catechism quotes, asks a son to help his father in his old age and not to grieve him, even if his mind fails. Then the commandment turns around. Parents have duties too: to see their children as children of God, to educate them, to be the first to hand on the faith, and to respect their freedom, including their calling in life. Paul writes in Ephesians: fathers, "provoke not your children to anger." And the circle widens to anyone with authority, which the Catechism says must be used as a service; Jesus tells his followers that whoever would be great among them must be their servant. Even Jesus, found in the temple at twelve, goes home to Nazareth with Mary and Joseph, and Luke says he "was subject to them." Honor flows up and down at once. The week in one breath: written in reason, his gift in us, the minimum not the maximum, God first, names are holy, keep holy the day, and now this.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a parent, a grandparent or an older person who looked after you, even imperfectly, and let one specific thing they did come back: a meal, a ride, a hard word that turned out right. If they're living, find the words you'd use to thank them; if they've died, thank them in silence; if the relationship is painful, choose another elder instead. If you pray, ask God to bless them.
Fourth commandment. Honor your father and mother: children honor and care for parents, and parents, and all in authority, serve those in their care. Today's word.
